cases.question: For a new NYC office under the 2022 codes, does a required exit door with a 31-inch clear opening meet the ordinary minimum width? There is no special door exception and its occupant load does not require a larger opening.
cases.expectedAnswer: No. Ordinary required minimum clear opening is 32 inches, subject to occupant-load capacity. Clear opening is not nominal door-leaf width.
cases.answerText: **No.** For the stated new NYC office and absent a special exception, the ordinary minimum clear width for a required door opening is **32 inches**; a 31-inch clear opening falls short by 1 inch (BC § 1010.1.1.1). The rule also requires sufficient capacity for the occupant load, but you state that load does not require a larger opening.
cases.operativeRuleReview: Correctly rejects a 31-inch required clear opening against the ordinary 32-inch minimum, with the supplied no-exception and occupant-load conditions accounted for. Full BC 1010.1.1.1 citation supplies the clear-opening rule and exceptions.

cases.question: For a new NYC office under the 2022 codes, may washbasins be supplied with tempered water instead of hot water? I am asking about the required type of supply, not its exact temperature.

cases.answerText:

cases.question: In a new NYC office under the 2022 codes, can ordinary mechanical exhaust air be discharged into the attic instead of outside? This is not a whole-house attic fan or a listed ductless cooking hood.
cases.expectedAnswer: No. Ordinary mechanical exhaust discharges outdoors; air must not be exhausted into an attic or crawl space. Stated exceptions do not apply.
cases.answerText:
**No.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, air removed by every mechanical exhaust system must be discharged outdoors, and air may not be exhausted into an attic or crawl space. The stated exceptions do not include ordinary office exhaust; the attic-fan exception is limited to whole-house ventilation-type attic fans serving dwelling units with private attics, and the domestic ductless-hood exception is separately limited. (MC § 501.3)

The separate outlet-location and separation requirements in MC § 501.3.1 apply to exhaust discharged outdoors; they do not authorize discharge into an attic. (MC § 501.3.1)
cases.operativeRuleReview: Correctly requires ordinary office exhaust outdoors and prohibits attic/crawl discharge under MC 501.3. Accurately limits its exceptions, and the full returned MC 501.3.1 outlet-location provision is not used to approve attic discharge.

cases.question: If we move that exhaust outside right beside the fresh-air intake, does reaching the exterior alone satisfy the rule?
cases.expectedAnswer: No. Exhaust discharge must not cause a nuisance and must be located so it cannot readily be drawn back in by a ventilating system; outlet distance provisions also apply.
cases.answerText: **No.** Reaching the exterior alone is not enough: the exhaust must be discharged where it will not cause a nuisance, cannot readily be drawn back into a ventilating system, and meet the applicable separation distances (MC § 501.3; MC § 501.3.1). For environmental-air exhaust outlets, the baseline separation is **10 feet from mechanical air intakes**. An outlet beside an intake would not meet that baseline unless the stated exception applies. The exception removes the 10-foot separation only for: Class 1 exhaust below 750 cfm serving a single room, dwelling, or sleeping unit; or Class 2 exhaust below 400 cfm serving a single dwelling or sleeping unit. In either case, combined energy-recovery cross-contamination and exhaust re-entrainment through the intake must be less than 10% of intake airflow, as established by the manufacturer. Without the exhaust classification, airflow, served space, and that system-condition information, whether the exception applies here is unresolved.
cases.operativeRuleReview: Correctly says outdoor discharge alone is insufficient; applies nuisance/re-entrainment and ordinary 10-foot environmental-exhaust intake separation. Added low-flow/Class1 or Class2 exception conditions and less-than10% combined cross-contamination/re-entrainment are supported by returned MC501.3.1 text. Does not assert that the unknown exception is met.

cases.question: In a commercial NYC vehicle service area under the 2022 codes, gasoline engines are run while vehicles remain stationary for diagnostics. Is general room ventilation enough, or is tailpipe capture also required?
cases.expectedAnswer: Source capture directly connected to motor-vehicle exhaust systems is additionally required, alongside mechanical ventilation. Capture must be engineered by a registered design professional or factory-built and designed/sized for the purpose.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, areas where motor vehicles operate require mechanical ventilation, and areas where vehicles are operated while stationary must additionally have source capture connected directly to the vehicle exhaust. Running gasoline engines while stationary for diagnostics therefore requires tailpipe capture; general room ventilation alone is not enough (MC § 502.14). The listed exceptions do not cover stationary diagnostic operation in a commercial service area: they concern electric vehicles, one- and two-family dwellings, or engines run only as long as needed to move vehicles into or out of the building.
cases.operativeRuleReview: The answer correctly says general room ventilation alone is insufficient for stationary gasoline-vehicle diagnostics. The full 2022 MC 502.14 passage requires mechanical ventilation under 403 plus directly connected source capture for stationary operation, with engineered or factory-built design. The named exceptions are scoped correctly.

cases.question: For a permanent open accessory parking facility in a NYC C4-2 commercial district, can we leave the surface as dusty bare soil?
cases.expectedAnswer: No. Grading, construction, surfacing and maintenance must provide adequate drainage and prevent dust. Permanent open accessory group parking requires permeable paving, asphaltic or Portland cement concrete, or another hard-surfaced dustless material.
cases.answerText: **No.** Dusty bare soil is not allowed for the stated open accessory off-street parking: ZR § 36-54 requires those spaces to be surfaced and maintained to prevent dust. If the facility meets ZR § 12-10’s definition of a “group parking facility,” the more specific permanent-use rule also requires permeable paving, asphaltic or Portland cement concrete, or another hard-surfaced dustless material; the question does not establish whether the facility meets that definition. The general rule also requires open accessory off-street parking spaces to be graded, constructed, surfaced, and maintained to provide adequate drainage and prevent dust. The question does not establish whether the facility has more than one parking space and common street access, conditions in the supplied definition of “group parking facility.”
cases.operativeRuleReview: The full current imported ZR 36-54 passage establishes C4 coverage, adequate drainage and dust prevention, and the permanent accessory group-parking surface alternatives. The answer correctly rejects dusty bare soil under the general rule without withholding that answer. Its separately cited 12-10 group-parking definition accurately qualifies the more specific permanent group-facility materials rule; the repetition is stylistic rather than a rule error.

cases.question: Would permeable paving be allowed, or must the surface be conventional asphalt?
cases.expectedAnswer: Permeable paving is expressly allowed; conventional asphalt is not mandatory. Adequate drainage and dust prevention still apply.
cases.answerText: **Permeable paving is expressly allowed; conventional asphalt is not the only option.** For an area used permanently as an open accessory *group parking facility*, ZR § 36-54 permits permeable paving, asphaltic or Portland cement concrete, or another hard-surfaced dustless material. The specific permanent-facility rule applies if the parking use meets ZR § 12-10’s definition of “group parking facility”: it must contain more than one parking space and have street access common to all spaces; if accessory to a residential use, it must also be designed to serve more than one dwelling unit. In any event, open accessory off-street parking must be graded, constructed, surfaced, and maintained to provide adequate drainage and prevent dust (ZR § 36-54).
cases.operativeRuleReview: The complete ZR 36-54 passage expressly lists permeable paving and does not mandate asphalt.
